threads.thread_goal: Align on current procedures and confirm scope of the integrated support programme.

messages.text: Morning all. To kick off the Integrated Early Support Programme for At-Risk Children, could we each share how we currently spot and refer children we are worried about? The idea is to pull this into the Current Procedures Mapping Document so we can complete task T1 and start shaping the Pilot Plan and Schedule in T9 and A7. Please include what you do in class or in the community, who you talk to, and any forms or systems you already use.

From the classroom side, I usually notice concerns through daily routines: small group activities, free play, and transitions. If a child shows repeated distress, withdrawal, or safety issues, I log notes in our class notebook and raise it with the class teacher the same day. For learning difficulties, I use our existing observation notes linked to curriculum objectives. If we both stay concerned, we bring it to the weekly staff meeting and sometimes ask the school leadership for guidance. There is no formal shared form with social services yet, which is a gap T1 and A1 should capture.

In my group, I mostly rely on informal talks with the teacher and quick chats with parents at pick-up. If I see repeated behaviour like hitting, very low energy, or hygiene concerns, I tell the teacher and we agree whether to note it in the class log. I am not always sure when this should go beyond the school to social services, so I think the mapping in A1 and the new protocol later will help. Right now, I do not use a specific checklist, just my own notes.

Similar to what was shared already. I observe during circle time, outdoor play, and meals. When I see patterns like frequent accidents, strong emotional outbursts, or a child not joining activities, I document short notes and discuss with the teacher. If we agree it is more than a short phase, we bring it to the special needs coordinator. There is an internal form we sometimes use, but it is not aligned with social work processes. That should be captured clearly in A1 under T1 so we can see overlaps and gaps.

From the community social work side, referrals usually come in through two routes: direct calls from parents or guardians, and written referrals from school leadership. For school referrals, we receive a short narrative email plus any existing notes. We then log the case in our social services system, assess urgency, and decide on next steps, which can include a home visit or a meeting at school. There is no shared early identification protocol yet, so T1 should document the current steps on both sides, and T9 and A7 will later define which classes and families are in the pilot.

Thanks all, this is helpful. For my current social work caseload linked to the school, I usually get involved only after the school leadership has already discussed the child internally. I then meet the parents at school, and if needed, open a case in our system. We do not have a standardised form that both school and social work use together. For T1 and A1, I can start drafting the social work side steps, but I will need one of you from the classroom to co-own the school side so we do not miss details.

I can co-own the school side of T1. I already have notes on our internal observation and referral steps, including when we involve the special needs coordinator and when we escalate to leadership. I suggest we structure A1 with two main sections: school procedures and social services procedures, then a short table of overlaps and gaps. Once we have a first draft, we can ask another assistant and one more social worker to review, as required in T1.

That sounds workable. To make it concrete: 427511 and 499701, could you confirm you are comfortable being listed as owners for completing A1 under T1? I can support by checking that the social work steps reflect our organisational guidelines and safeguarding rules. Once A1 is ready, we can use it as input for T9 and A7 when we define the pilot scope.

Yes, I am ok to be listed as co-owner for T1 and A1 on the social work side. I will start by writing out the current referral path from school leadership to social services, including how we record consent and what information we usually request. I will share a draft for comments before we finalise.

Confirmed from my side as well. I will map the classroom and school steps: how assistants observe, how we document, when we involve teachers, special needs coordinator, and leadership. I will also note where we already talk to parents so that later T4 and T5 can build on that. Once we merge our parts, we can highlight where the process is unclear or duplicated.

Happy to review the school section of A1 once you have a draft. I can check that it matches what happens in my class and add any missing steps, especially around informal conversations with parents and how we handle minor incidents that do not yet need a referral.

I can also add examples from my group once the draft of A1 is ready. Sometimes we see social issues at home through what children say or how they arrive at school, and I want to make sure those situations are reflected in the mapping so they are not missed in the new programme.

On pilot scope for T9 and A7: my initial thought is to start with two kindergarten classes where we already have some children with known concerns, plus one class with fewer current cases to see how early identification works. That would give us roughly 15 to 20 children who might need closer monitoring, but we would not limit the programme only to existing cases. Does that feel manageable from the classroom side within one school term?

From a workload and classroom management perspective, two classes with existing concerns plus one lower-need class sounds reasonable, as long as the observation tools and routines are quick to use. If we assume around 5 to 7 children per class who might need closer attention, that is still feasible if checklists can be done in a few minutes per child. I would avoid going beyond three classes in this first term so we can test and adjust without overloading staff.

Agree with keeping it to three classes. It will also make it easier to run short check-ins and use the monitoring template later without creating too much admin. I suggest we include at least one class where there is a strong relationship with parents already, to help with family engagement during the pilot.

I am ok with three classes as long as we are clear which types of cases are in scope. For example, will we include only children with repeated wellbeing or safety concerns, or also milder learning difficulties? It would help me to know what to flag during daily routines.

Good point. For the pilot scope, I propose we include: 1) children with repeated wellbeing or safety concerns, such as frequent injuries, strong emotional outbursts, or signs of neglect; and 2) children with emerging learning difficulties that significantly affect participation in daily activities. We would not include very mild, short-term issues unless they persist over several weeks. This scope would apply across the three selected classes and will be reflected in T9 and A7.

That scope works for me. To summarise: we will pilot in three kindergarten classes, focusing on children with repeated wellbeing or safety concerns and those with clear emerging learning difficulties that affect participation. Mild, short-term issues will be monitored but not formally included unless they persist. This gives us a clear frame for T9 and A7 and should keep the workload manageable.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the early identification and referral protocol and observation checklist.

messages.text: I have uploaded a draft of the Early Identification and Referral Protocol as A2, based on the mapping in A1 and task T2. It sets out roles, steps, and consent requirements, and I tried to align it with safeguarding and data protection rules. Alongside this, 499701 has drafted a Classroom Observation Checklist for Early Signs as A3 under T3. Could school colleagues review both and comment on whether the steps and checklist items fit daily practice and existing kindergarten procedures? We also need to think about how often A3 should be used.

Quick overview of A3: it has three sections that can be completed in about five minutes per child. 1) Behaviour indicators, such as withdrawal, aggression, or difficulty following routines. 2) Learning indicators, like persistent trouble with basic tasks linked to curriculum objectives. 3) Safety indicators, including frequent accidents or signs of neglect. The idea is that assistants or teachers can use it when they have a concern, not for every child every week. Please flag anything that feels unclear or too time-consuming.

I read through A3 and it looks helpful, but I am a bit unsure about when exactly to start using it. For example, if a child has two difficult mornings in a row, should I already fill in the checklist, or wait longer? It would help me if A2 and A3 together gave a simple rule of thumb so I know when to move from informal notes to the formal checklist.

From my reading, A3 is manageable if we use it when there is a pattern, not for every small incident. I suggest we add a short line at the top: use the checklist when concerns persist for at least one week or when there is a serious safety incident. That would keep it aligned with our current practice and avoid extra workload, which is important for T11 when we check alignment with existing procedures.

Good question. In A2, I proposed that the formal process starts when there are either repeated concerns over at least one week or a single serious safety event. We can mirror that in A3. So the flow would be: informal notes and discussion first, then A3 when the concern is ongoing or serious, then the referral steps in A2 if the checklist confirms the concern. I can update A2 and A3 to make this clearer.

On A2, I noticed that the consent section might need a bit more detail about how we explain information sharing to parents. Right now it says we obtain written consent, but in practice we often start with a conversation and then follow up with a form. Could we add a short script or bullet points in A2 so assistants and teachers know what to say before they involve social services?

Agreed, that is a good catch. I will add a short explanation section in A2 that outlines how staff should talk to parents about the programme and consent, making sure it stays within safeguarding and data protection rules. We can later align that wording with the family engagement materials in A5 under T4 so parents hear consistent messages.

On frequency of using A3, I would suggest we agree that for the pilot we complete it: 1) when a concern has lasted at least one week, and 2) then repeat it every two to three weeks for children already identified, so we can track change without overloading staff. That rhythm should also fit with the monitoring template later.

I can work with that schedule. Completing A3 when a concern lasts a week and then every two to three weeks for those children feels realistic. It also gives us enough data points to see if the classroom support routines in A4 later are helping.

Thanks, that makes it clearer for me. I will follow that rule in my class: start A3 after a week of concern or a serious incident, then repeat every few weeks. It would be helpful if this is written in bold at the top of A3 so everyone remembers.

I have now updated A2 and A3 with: 1) clearer triggers for when to use the checklist, 2) a short explanation for parents about consent and information sharing, and 3) a simple flow from classroom observation to referral. From a social work perspective, the steps are workable and align with our organisational guidelines. Before we say it is final for the pilot, can school colleagues confirm that A2 fits with existing kindergarten procedures and does not conflict with any school rules under T11?

I checked A2 against our current kindergarten procedures. The roles and steps match what we already do, with the addition of the structured checklist and clearer consent wording. I do not see any conflicts with school rules. The only small point is that we should make sure leadership is aware of the new flow, but that can be handled when we present the pilot plan.

I also reviewed A2 and it looks consistent with how we usually involve social services, just more structured. The consent section is clearer now, and I think assistants will find the step-by-step list helpful. From my side, I am comfortable using this protocol in the pilot.

Same here. A2 fits with our daily routines and does not add unnecessary meetings. The link between A3 and the referral steps is clear. I suggest we confirm A2 as the protocol for the pilot so we can move on to training materials.

Thanks all. To summarise this thread: 1) We will use A3 when concerns last at least one week or after a serious safety incident, then repeat every two to three weeks for identified children. 2) A2, with the updated consent and flow sections, is approved for use in the pilot and aligns with existing school and social work procedures under T11. I will mark T2 as moving towards completion and coordinate with 427511 on training content in T7.

threads.thread_goal: Define classroom support routines and align them with school procedures and workload.

messages.text: I have drafted a set of classroom support routines for identified at-risk children and added them into A4 under task T6. There are eight strategies, such as predictable visual schedules, calm corners, small-group support for key activities, and planned check-ins during transitions. Each is designed to fit within existing classroom management rules and curriculum objectives. Could you review and say which ones feel realistic in your classes, and if anything important is missing? We also need to think about how these routines link to the staff feedback process in A8 and T10.

I like the idea of a calm corner and visual schedules in A4, but I am not sure how to manage the planned check-ins during busy times like arrival and lunch. Sometimes I am already stretched with basic care tasks. Maybe we could suggest a minimum number of check-ins per day so it stays realistic.

In my class, the visual schedule and calm corner are already partly in place, so formalising them in A4 makes sense. For planned check-ins, I usually tie them to existing routines: greeting at arrival, a quick word before outdoor play, and a short check at the end of the day. That gives at least two or three touchpoints without adding separate tasks. Maybe we can write it that way in A4 so it feels integrated rather than extra.

From a social work perspective, the routines in A4 look supportive of social-emotional needs, especially the calm corner, emotion naming, and predictable transitions. I would just suggest we add a short note that these routines should be adapted for each child and that any significant changes in behaviour are recorded in the monitoring template later. That will help us see if the routines are having an effect.

I am wondering about the small-group support strategy in A4. For some classes, we do not always have enough adults to run extra small groups. Should we mark that one as optional, to be used when staffing allows, so that assistants do not feel they are failing if they cannot do it every day?

Good point. We can mark small-group support as a flexible strategy in A4, to be used when staffing and class size allow. The core set could then be: visual schedules, calm corner, planned check-ins tied to existing routines, and simple emotion coaching. The others can be listed as additional options. That might help us keep to the 5 to 8 practical strategies target in T6 without overcommitting.

If we treat small-group support as optional, I feel more confident. For the core set, I would vote for: 1) visual schedule, 2) calm corner, 3) planned check-ins linked to routines, 4) simple emotion coaching, and 5) clear safety rules reminders before higher-risk activities like outdoor play. Those are things I can realistically do every day.

I agree with that core set. I would add one more: a short daily check of seating or grouping to make sure at-risk children are placed where they can get support and feel safe. That would bring us to six core strategies, with small-group work and extra communication with parents as optional ones.

From my side, that list of six core strategies covers the main social-emotional and safety needs we see in cases. If we document them clearly in A4 with short examples, it should also make it easier to explain to parents what support their child is getting in class.

I will update A4 so that the selected core strategies are: 1) visual schedule, 2) calm corner, 3) planned check-ins linked to existing routines, 4) emotion coaching, 5) safety rule reminders before higher-risk activities, and 6) daily seating or grouping check. Small-group support and extra parent communication will be listed as optional. That should meet the T6 requirement of 5 to 8 practical strategies.

On documentation and storage: do we want A4 to live in the same shared folder as A2 and A3, or should we also have a printed version in each classroom? Some assistants are more comfortable with paper guidelines they can glance at quickly.

I would suggest both: a digital version of A4 in the shared project folder alongside A2, A3, and A8, plus a one-page summary printed for each pilot classroom. That way, updates can be made centrally, but day-to-day use is easy. We can note in the guideline that the digital version is the official one.

Linking this to T10 and A8, we could also add a short section in the Staff Feedback and Check-in Process that asks assistants to share which routines from A4 they are using and what is working or not. That would help us refine the routines during the pilot.

So for documentation and storage, can we agree on: 1) A4 stored digitally in the shared project folder with A2, A3, and A8 as the master version, and 2) a one-page printed summary of the core strategies in each pilot classroom. Any updates will be made in the digital version and reprinted if needed. This should keep things simple and accessible.
That works for me. Having a printed summary in the classroom will make it easier to remember the routines during busy times, and I know where to look online if I need more detail.
Agreed. With the core strategies confirmed and the storage approach clear, we can start using A4 in the three pilot classes once the printed summaries are ready.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on family engagement approach and home visit criteria.

messages.text: I have drafted the family engagement script and leaflet text as A5 under T4, and 361403 has prepared initial criteria for home visits under T5. The script explains the programme in simple language and how we work together with parents, and the leaflet mirrors that. The home visit criteria focus on safety and wellbeing concerns plus low engagement. Could you review and share if the wording feels clear and respectful, and whether the visit criteria and safety rules are realistic from your perspective?

To add some detail: the home visit criteria in T5 currently include: 1) repeated safety or neglect concerns, 2) serious wellbeing issues where we need to understand the home context, and 3) very low family engagement despite several attempts to meet at school. The safety rules cover visiting in pairs when there is any known risk, logging visit details, and respecting working hours. I would appreciate feedback from the classroom side on how this fits with your contact with parents.

On A5, the script is generally clear and uses parent-friendly language. One suggestion: early in the conversation, could we emphasise that the programme is about support, not blame, and that we work together with families? That might help reduce anxiety when we first introduce it, especially for parents who have had difficult experiences with services before.

I like that the leaflet in A5 explains things simply, but I am not sure how to handle questions about data sharing. Parents sometimes ask exactly who will see information about their child. Could we add a short line that says information is only shared between the school and social services team involved in the programme, and only with consent, except in serious safety situations?

From my experience, parents respond better when we give concrete examples. Maybe A5 could include one short example of how the programme might look for a child: for instance, extra support in class, regular check-ins, and a meeting with a social worker if needed. That might make the leaflet feel more real and less abstract.

We can definitely add a clear line on data sharing in A5, consistent with the consent section in A2. I will check the wording against our organisational guidelines to make sure it is accurate and still easy to understand. We should also mention that in rare cases of serious risk, we may need to act without consent, so expectations are honest.

I will rework the opening of the script in A5 to stress partnership and support, and add a short example as suggested. I will also coordinate with 361403 to align the data sharing explanation with A2 and our guidelines. Once updated, I will flag it here for a quick final check before we say it is ready for the pilot.

On the home visit criteria in T5, the three points you listed make sense. I would just add that before suggesting a home visit, we should usually try at least one meeting at school at a time that works for the family. That might reduce the number of visits needed and respect the constraint about limited availability outside core hours.
I agree. Many parents I talk to prefer meeting at school first. Maybe A5 could also say that home visits are one option, not something that will always happen, so families do not feel pressured.

That is a good safeguard. I will update T5 so that the standard sequence is: 1) offer a school-based meeting at a suitable time, 2) if concerns remain or engagement is very low, consider a home visit based on the criteria, and 3) always follow safety procedures, including visiting in pairs when needed and logging the visit. This should keep visits focused and safe.

From the classroom side, that sequence feels respectful and realistic. It also gives us a clear message to share with parents: we start with school meetings and only suggest home visits when it really helps understanding or safety.

I have now updated A5 with: 1) a stronger emphasis on support and partnership, 2) a simple example of what the programme might look like for a child, and 3) a clear line on information sharing and consent, aligned with A2 and our guidelines. Could assistants confirm that the wording feels natural for conversations at the door or during meetings?

I have read the updated A5 and it feels natural to use. The explanation of support and consent is clear, and the example makes it easier to describe the programme. From my side, I am comfortable using this script and leaflet in the pilot.
Same here. The wording is simple enough for quick conversations, and the line about who sees the information will help when parents ask. I am ok with using A5 as it is now.
I also support using the updated A5 for the pilot. It matches how we usually talk with parents and adds clarity about the programme and consent.

With the updated sequence and safety rules in T5, I am confident we have clear and safe criteria for home visits and community follow-up. To summarise: home visits are considered when there are repeated safety or neglect concerns, serious wellbeing issues needing home context, or very low engagement after school-based attempts, and we always follow the safety procedures. Unless anyone objects, I suggest we confirm these criteria for the pilot.
Agreed. The criteria and safety rules in T5 are clear and workable for the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in monitoring indicators, reporting template, and pilot start date.

messages.text: I have drafted the Monitoring and Reporting Template as A6 under T8, along with proposed indicators for T12. The template has sections for wellbeing, learning, and safety, plus space for classroom routines used and any social work actions. The indicators I suggest are: 1) number of recorded safety incidents, 2) attendance patterns, 3) observed wellbeing using a simple rating, 4) participation in key classroom activities, and 5) family engagement level. Please review A6 and share if the fields are clear and not too heavy to complete.

Looking at A6, the structure makes sense. For the wellbeing rating, I suggest we use a simple three-point scale with short descriptions, so assistants do not have to think too long about numbers. Also, could we pre-fill the list of classroom routines from A4 so we just tick which ones are used for each child?

I like that A6 combines wellbeing, learning, and safety, but I am a bit worried about how often we need to fill it in. If it is too frequent, it might be hard to keep up. Could we agree on a realistic frequency, maybe linked to when we update the observation checklist A3?

I would support aligning the A6 updates with the A3 schedule. For example, we could complete A6 for each identified child every two to three weeks, at the same time we repeat the checklist. That would give us regular data without daily paperwork.
On the family engagement indicator, could we give examples of what low, medium, and high engagement look like? That might help assistants and social workers rate it in a similar way.

I can adjust A6 so that: 1) the wellbeing rating uses a three-point scale with short descriptions, and 2) the classroom routines section lists the core strategies from A4 with tick boxes. For frequency, aligning with the A3 schedule every two to three weeks for identified children sounds reasonable and fits the T12 requirement for clear data collection frequency.

For family engagement in A6, we could define: low as rarely responding or attending despite several invitations, medium as sometimes attending or responding, and high as regularly attending meetings and communicating proactively. Short examples next to each label should help keep ratings consistent.

If we only complete A6 every two to three weeks for each identified child, I feel more confident about keeping up. The tick boxes for routines will also make it faster. I am ok with the five indicators you proposed as long as the template stays on one or two pages per child.
Same here. The indicators cover what we need to know, and the frequency and format feel manageable. I suggest we confirm these five indicators for the pilot and add them clearly at the top of A6.

Ok, I will finalise A6 with the five indicators: safety incidents, attendance, wellbeing rating, participation in key activities, and family engagement level, plus the tick boxes for routines. Data will be recorded every two to three weeks for each identified child. That should complete T12 and move T8 close to done.

With A2, A3, A4, and A5 now agreed, and A6 almost final, we should check if we are ready to set a pilot start date in A7. Are there any remaining gaps that would stop us starting in two weeks, assuming we can brief staff using the training session from T7?

From the classroom side, starting in two weeks is possible if we receive the printed summaries of A4, the final A3 and A6 templates, and a short briefing session. That timing also gives us a bit of space to talk with parents using A5 before we begin full monitoring.

I am comfortable with a start in two weeks as well, as long as we know exactly which three classes are in the pilot and have a clear list of the children we will monitor more closely. That will help me plan my time.
Two weeks works for me. It would be helpful if A7 includes a simple calendar with key dates: training, start of observations, first feedback check-in, and a mid-pilot review.

Based on T9 and A7, I propose we confirm the pilot scope and start date as follows: three kindergarten classes, focusing on children with repeated wellbeing or safety concerns and emerging learning difficulties as agreed earlier, with the pilot starting in two weeks on a Monday. We will run it for one school term, with the first staff training session in the week before. Unless there are objections, I will update A7 accordingly.
That summary matches my understanding. With A2 and A3 already approved and A4, A5, and A6 ready, I am comfortable confirming the pilot scope and start date as you described.

One last check: the monitoring indicators in A6 do not require any changes to the protocol in A2, so we can keep the protocol as previously approved. I will note in A7 that A2 is final for the pilot and that any learning from the monitoring will be used for later adjustments, not during this short term unless there is a serious issue.
Agreed. No changes to A2 are needed based on A6. We can go ahead with the protocol as it stands for the pilot.
